question: How does the paper define a reference alternative?
ground_truth_answer: An alternative is defined as a reference alternative if and only if it is 'attention privileged,' meaning it is always paid attention to whenever it is in the menu. References are also assumed to be menu-independent.
answer: A reference alternative is defined as an alternative that is attention privileged, meaning it is always paid attention to [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 2]. In the context of a reference-dependent attention function, an alternative is a reference if and only if it is attention privileged, regardless of how it attained such a privilege [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 5]. The paper also states that the reference alternatives are exactly those alternatives that are always paid attention to [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 1].

Random Attention and Unobserved Reference

Alternatives∗

Varun Bansal†

January 3, 2025

arXiv:2407.01528v3  [econ.TH]  1 Jan 2025

Abstract

In this paper, I develop and characterize a random attention model with un-
observed reference alternatives.
The decision-maker pays attention to different
subsets of the available set of alternatives randomly. The reference alternatives are
exactly those alternatives that are always paid attention to, i.e. they are attention-
privileged. These alternatives are unknown to the outside observer. The character-
ization allows for a complete identification of the reference alternatives and a coarse
identification of the underlying preferences. I then restrict the model by considering
the independent random attention function and provide a complete identification
of the underlying preferences.

Keywords: Bounded Rationality, Stochastic Choice, Limited Attention, Consid-
eration Sets

Introduction

Decision-making is often constrained by limited attention, whether due to cognitive pro-
cessing limits caused by the availability of too many alternatives or a shortage of time.
In such situations, decision-makers (DM) often resort to heuristics that can help them
decide relatively quickly with less mental exercise. If the DM has to make similar choices
multiple times with the same underlying primitives, the heuristic that decides how to
allocate attention can lead to different choices.
Stochastic choice functions represent
such choices, with the main research task then being to ascertain the likely underlying
heuristic and the primitives that drive the decisions of the DM. Cattaneo et al. (2020)

Characterization

In the present section I characterize the RAM-UR by using three testable axioms. These
axioms restrict how the choices behave across different menus.

Existence of a Dominant Alternative (EDA): For each A ∈X : p(x, A) = 0 for
some x ∈A∗implies p(y, {x, y}) = 1 for some y ∈A \ {x}.

A DM with limited attention fails to choose an alternative in two cases. First, if that
alternative is never considered. Second, if whenever it is considered, it is dominated by
another alternative. EDA says that, the only way an alternative is never chosen is if
another alternative always dominates it and is always considered in the binary choice
between the two. This means that it is not possible for an alternative to never be cho-
sen just because it is never considered, making each alternative to be non-trivial in the
problem. The axiom also says that the set of possible consideration sets is rich enough
that the only way an alternative is never chosen is if another dominating alternative is
always considered, i.e. it is attention privileged. This way, EDA captures the essence of
the modified full support assumption.

Certainty WARP (C-WARP): For all x ∈X∗and y ∈X with {x, y} ⊆A∗⊆X∗:
p(y, A) = 1 implies p(x, A′) = 0 for all A′ ⊆X with {x, y} ⊆A′∗⊆X∗.

In certain cases, it is logical to assume that the reference is observable. For instance,
for a DM in the market for a new car, their current car can be a reference. However,
in many situations, it is not realistic to assume the knowledge of the DM’s reference to
anyone else but the DM themselves. Further, to analyze a choice problem with observ-
able references, we have to deal with a family of stochastic choice functions, as done by
Kovach and Suleymanov (2023). The inputs for the stochastic choice functions in their
model were pairs of subsets1 and references- one family of stochastic choice function for
each alternative as the reference. This is quite a significant data requirement. If we re-
strict the references to be unknown, we deal with just a single stochastic choice function
over menus and thus, we do not have to deal with families of stochastic choice functions
for each possible reference.

It is also not obvious that a reference alternative must be unique. In what follows, I
allow for multiple reference alternatives; clearly, one particular such alternative could be
the status quo. In this spirit, I define an alternative to be a reference alternative if and
only if it is attention privileged, i.e. it is always paid attention to. Since I am looking at
choices from menus that depend on unobservable reference alternatives, I assume that the
references are menu-independent. It is certainly plausible that references can be menu-
dependent, through which we can explain a larger set of stochastic choice behavior, but
dealing with menu-dependent unobservable references is beyond the scope of this paper.
I provide below three examples that match the mentioned assumptions.

In the literature discussed above, a general theme is that the primitives include the refer-
ence point. It is natural to challenge the assumption of the observability of the reference
point. Ok et al. (2015) and Tserenjigmid (2019) are two relevant papers here. However,
in Tserenjigmid (2019) the references are not alternatives but a vector of attributes which
depend upon the minimum of those attributes among the alternatives in any menu. It is
thus, menu dependent as well. Kovach and Suleymanov (2023) is the first paper to study
reference dependence in a stochastic setting, which makes the current work the first to
study unobservable references in this setup.

We have assumed menu-independence with respect to the references. In Kovach and Suleymanov
(2023), the input to the problem is menu-reference pairs so the question of menu inde-
pendence was moot. However, it is possible to allow for menu-dependent unobservable
references as a possible extension to the model in the current paper.

question: Does the model allow a decision maker to have more than one reference alternative?
ground_truth_answer: Yes, the framework allows for multiple reference alternatives; the status quo is given as one example of a possible reference alternative.
answer: Yes, the model allows a decision-maker to have more than one reference alternative [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 2]. The model explicitly states that multiple reference alternatives or no reference alternatives can be present in any menu [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 5]. An alternative is defined as a reference alternative if and only if it is attention privileged, meaning it is always paid attention to [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 2]. For example, past choices of a decision-maker can act as multiple unobservable references [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 3].

while the IRA model is itself a boundary case of the RAM-UR-IRA3.

with unobservable references if and only if it satisfies EDA, C-WARP and EXP.

Even with limited data about choices from menus, in most cases we can identify the

question: Why might it be reasonable to assume a reference alternative directs attention?
ground_truth_answer: It is reasonable because when a decision maker applies a heuristic under limited attention, a reference alternative can plausibly direct where that attention goes; prior work provides a characterization of a reference-dependent random attention model along with special cases in which the attention function is further restricted.
answer: It is plausible to suppose that a reference alternative “captures” the decision‑maker’s focus because, under limited‑attention heuristics, the DM tends to give priority to those alternatives that are **attention‑privileged**.  In the RAM literature a reference alternative is defined precisely as an alternative that is always included in the consideration set whenever it appears in the menu — i.e., it enjoys “attention privilege” (see Definition 4) 【Random_Attention.pdf, Page 5】.  Consequently, when a heuristic that allocates attention only to a subset of the menu is used, the presence of a reference alternative will automatically draw the DM’s attention to it.  This intuition is explicitly noted by Kovach and Suleymanov (2023), who argue that “it is reasonable to assume that a reference alternative can direct attention when the underlying heuristic is applied due to limited attention” 【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 1‑2】.  Thus, because reference alternatives are always considered and limited‑attention decision‑makers rely on simple heuristics, assuming that a reference alternative directs attention is a natural modeling choice.

choices of a DM. In particular, Kovach and Suleymanov (2023) uses the framework of
RAM to look at how a reference alternative, or a status quo in their case, can affect

question: In the shoe-brand example, why does a favorite athlete's endorsed brand count as a menu-independent reference?
ground_truth_answer: It stays as a reference whenever the decision maker faces any shoe choice, so it does not depend on the particular menu presented, and it does not stop the decision maker from also having another favorite athlete, which allows for multiple reference alternatives.
answer: In the shoe-brand example, an Air Jordan shoe, associated with Michael Jordan, is considered a menu-independent reference because it is likely to remain a reference whenever the Decision Maker (DM) has to make a shoe choice [Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 2-3].

question: What is 'Example 2' in the paper about, and what point does it illustrate about references?

answer:

In most cases, unique identification of the set of references is possible, for example, if choice probabilities are available from all two and three-element menus, even without data on singleton sets [Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 6-7].

There is a rare exception where identification might not be complete: if the second least preferred alternative is not a reference but the least preferred alternative is. Overall, the model allows for a complete identification of the reference alternatives [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 1].

Introduction

Decision-making is often constrained by limited attention, whether due to cognitive pro-
cessing limits caused by the availability of too many alternatives or a shortage of time.
In such situations, decision-makers (DM) often resort to heuristics that can help them
decide relatively quickly with less mental exercise. If the DM has to make similar choices
multiple times with the same underlying primitives, the heuristic that decides how to
allocate attention can lead to different choices.
Stochastic choice functions represent

heuristic and the primitives that drive the decisions of the DM. Cattaneo et al. (2020)

question: Why does C-WARP hold when an alternative is always chosen from a menu?
ground_truth_answer: If an alternative y is always chosen in a menu, it must be attention-privileged and better than every other alternative; if it weren't better, the full support assumption would imply the other alternative would be chosen with positive probability, which contradicts y always being chosen. Hence C-WARP is satisfied.
answer: If an alternative, say y, is always chosen in a menu, then it is considered attention-privileged and is better than any other alternative. This is because if it were not better, the full support assumption would imply that another alternative would be chosen with a positive probability. Therefore, C-WARP will be satisfied under this condition [Random_Attention.pdf, Page 13].

Certainty WARP captures the idea that if an alternative is revealed to be dominated

there exists an attention-privileged alternative that dominates each alternative in the
union of these menus. If we look at two attention-privileged alternatives, they will both
be always considered, so the preference will determine which will be chosen, but it will be
chosen with certainty in the union. It is in some ways similar to the expansion condition
of Manzini and Mariotti (2007) in that it deals with the union of two menus. However,
it works with any two menus with certain choices. It is silent on menus where certain
choice is not observed.

Theorem 1 A stochastic choice function is representable by a random attention model
with unobservable references if and only if it satisfies EDA, C-WARP and EXP.

It is worth mentioning that one can reach multiple representations of a stochastic choice
function by slightly changing the constructed attention function. However, in each rep-
resentation, the set of reference alternatives will be uniquely identified.

Even with limited data about choices from menus, in most cases we can identify the
set of references uniquely. For instance, if there is no data available on singleton sets
but we have the choice probabilities from all two and three-element menus, identification
will be mostly possible. A rare exception is the case where the second least preferred
alternative is not a reference but the least preferred alternative is. In such a case, we
will not be able to ascertain which of the two will be the least preferred (and hence, a
reference) and which is the second least preferred. However, we will be able to identify
all other reference alternatives uniquely.

The most important identification result is that we are only able to identify the pref-
erences coarsely, i.e.
we can identify the relative ranking of an alternative (whether
a reference or not) with respect to all reference alternatives and the transitive closure
of the partial order constructed through this relative ranking.

reference alternatives, we are not able to identify the preference and thus, one can repre-
sent the choice function by taking any extension (Szpilrajn (1930)) of the revealed strict
partial order7. The coarse identification is the result of the restrictions on both the ob-
servability of the references and on the amount of data available.

answer:
In the sub‑cases where the first alternative \(a\) belongs to the revealed reference set \(\bar E\) (i.e., \(a\in\bar E\)), the proof obtains the strict preference \(a\succ c\) by a two‑step use of the **EXP** (ex‑post choice) axiom and the **REG** (regularity) axiom.

1. **Start from the binary choices that involve the reference alternatives.**  
   Because \(a\) and \(b\) are both in \(\bar E\) we have  
   \[
   p(a,\{a,b\})=1\quad\text{and}\quad p(b,\{b,c\})=1 .
   \]  
   (see the case “\(a\in\bar E,\;b\in\bar E,\;c\in X,\;a\succ b\) and \(b\succ c\)” in the proof)【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 18-19】.

2. **Apply EXP to the three‑element menu \(\{a,b,c\}\).**  
   EXP states that when the antecedent holds, exactly one of the alternatives receives probability 1 in the larger menu. Hence either  
   \[
   p(a,\{a,b,c\})=1\quad\text{or}\quad p(b,\{a,b,c\})=1 .
   \]  
   (same passage)【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 18-19】.

3. **Rule out the second possibility by REG.**  
   If \(p(b,\{a,b,c\})=1\), then by REG we must also have \(p(b,\{a,b\})=1\).  
   But \(p(b,\{a,b\})=1\) contradicts the earlier fact that \(a\succ b\) (which required \(p(a,\{a,b\})=1\)). Therefore the alternative \(b\) cannot obtain probability 1 in the three‑element menu.

4. **Conclude that \(p(a,\{a,b,c\})=1\).**  
   The only remaining possibility from step 2 is that \(a\) receives probability 1 in \(\{a,b,c\}\).

5. **Use REG again to drop \(b\) from the menu.**  
   REG implies that if an alternative has probability 1 in a larger menu, it also has probability 1 in any sub‑menu that contains it. Hence  
   \[
   p(a,\{a,c\})=1 .
   \]  
   (the proof explicitly states “By REG again, we have \(p(a,\{a,c\})=1\) and thus, \(a\succ c\) holds.”)【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 18-19】.

6. **Translate the choice probability into the preference relation.**  
   By definition of the binary relation used in the proof, \(p(a,\{a,c\})=1\) is equivalent to the strict preference \(a\succ c\).

Thus, in every case where \(a\) is a reference alternative, the combination of EXP (which forces a unique probability‑1 choice in the larger menu) and REG (which propagates that probability‑1 choice to smaller menus) yields the conclusion \(a\succ c\).

answer:
The argument proceeds by contradiction.  
In the case where both \(a\) and \(b\) belong to the “elite’’ set \(\bar E\) (so that \(a\succ b\)), the **EXP** axiom tells us that either  

\[
p(a,\{a,b,c\})=1\quad\text{or}\quad p(b,\{a,b,c\})=1 .
\]

The proof assumes the second alternative, \(p(b,\{a,b,c\})=1\), and then applies the **REG** (regularity) axiom.  REG implies that if an alternative is chosen with probability 1 from a larger menu, it must also be chosen with probability 1 from any sub‑menu that contains it.  Hence  

\[
p(b,\{a,b\})=1 .
\]

But this is impossible because the strict preference \(a\succ b\) requires \(p(a,\{a,b\})=1\) and therefore \(p(b,\{a,b\})=0\).  The contradiction shows that the assumption \(p(b,\{a,b,c\})=1\) cannot hold, and consequently the only remaining possibility is that \(p(a,\{a,b,c\})>0\) (in fact, \(p(a,\{a,b,c\})=1\)).  

**Citation:** The contradiction is spelled out in the proof of Case 2: “Suppose, \(p(b,\{a,b,c\}) = 1\). Then by REG, \(p(b,\{a,b\}) = 1\) … however, this contradicts the fact that \(a \succ b\) and thus, \(p(a,\{a,b,c\}) = 1\) should hold” [Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 19‑20].

ground_truth_answer: By RIIA, p(c,{a,c}) equals p(c,{a,b,c}). Assuming the latter is positive leads, via R-IND, to a ratio that contradicts R-ASYM, so p(c,{a,b,c}) must equal 0. This in turn (via RIIA and Lemma 3) forces p(a,{a,c}) = 1, establishing that a â‰» c.
answer:
The model sets the probability of choosing **c** from the three‑element menu to zero by invoking the **Regularity (REG)** axiom together with the assumption that **c** is never chosen when the menu is only \(\{b,c\}\).

* In the proof on pages 20‑22 the author writes:  

  “*Note that \(p(c,\{a,b,c\}) = 0\) by REG since \(p(c,\{b,c\}) = 0\) by assumption*”【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 20-22】.  

  REG states that adding alternatives to a menu cannot increase the choice probability of any alternative; therefore, if \(c\) has zero probability in the smaller menu \(\{b,c\}\), it must also have zero probability in any larger menu that contains \(\{b,c\}\), such as \(\{a,b,c\}\).

* This zero‑probability result is then used to deduce the ordering of preferences. Because \(p(c,\{a,b,c\}) = 0\) while the total probability must sum to one, the model concludes that the other alternatives must have positive choice probabilities:  

  “*Since \(p(c,\{a,b,c\}) = 0\) and \(p(a^{*},\{a,b,c\}) = 0\) (by Lemma 3), we have \(p(b,\{a,b,c\}) > 0\)*”【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 20-22】.  

  Combining this with the asymmetry and independence‑of‑irrelevant‑alternatives (R‑ASYM, R‑IND) axioms yields  

  “*…\(p(a,\{a,c\})/p(a,\{a,b,c\}) = 1\) … By R‑IND … we obtain \(a \succ c\)*”【Random_Attention.pdf, Pages 20-22】.

Thus, establishing \(p(c,\{a,b,c\}) = 0\) serves two purposes:

1. **It follows directly from REG** because \(c\) is already excluded from the smaller menu \(\{b,c\}\).  
2. **It forces the model to assign positive probability to the other alternatives**, which, together with the other axioms, leads to the inference that **\(a\) is strictly preferred to \(c\) (\(a \succ c\))**. This contributes to the overall strict total order over the set of alternatives (e.g., \(a \succ b \succ c\) in the examples given).

Random Attention and Unobserved Reference

Alternatives∗

Varun Bansal†

January 3, 2025

arXiv:2407.01528v3  [econ.TH]  1 Jan 2025

Abstract

In this paper, I develop and characterize a random attention model with un-
observed reference alternatives.
The decision-maker pays attention to different
subsets of the available set of alternatives randomly. The reference alternatives are
exactly those alternatives that are always paid attention to, i.e. they are attention-
privileged. These alternatives are unknown to the outside observer. The character-
ization allows for a complete identification of the reference alternatives and a coarse
identification of the underlying preferences. I then restrict the model by considering
the independent random attention function and provide a complete identification
of the underlying preferences.

JEL Classification: D01, D91, Z13

Keywords: Bounded Rationality, Stochastic Choice, Limited Attention, Consid-
eration Sets

1
Introduction

Decision-making is often constrained by limited attention, whether due to cognitive pro-
cessing limits caused by the availability of too many alternatives or a shortage of time.
In such situations, decision-makers (DM) often resort to heuristics that can help them
decide relatively quickly with less mental exercise. If the DM has to make similar choices
multiple times with the same underlying primitives, the heuristic that decides how to
allocate attention can lead to different choices.
Stochastic choice functions represent
such choices, with the main research task then being to ascertain the likely underlying
heuristic and the primitives that drive the decisions of the DM. Cattaneo et al. (2020)

The idea of reference-dependent choice has also been the focus of several papers. Masatlioglu and Ok
(2005) and Masatlioglu and Ok (2014) are seminal papers in this area. These authors
were one of the first to model status quo bias in choice, which is a widely observed be-
havior in experiments on individual choice11. Sagi (2006) imposes a no-regret condition
on the reference dependent preferences and Tapkı (2007) allows for incomplete reference
dependent preferences.
Note that all mentioned works model the effect of the status
quo on preferences. However, it is possible that the status quo might affect attention
as well. Dean et al. (2017) looks at status quo bias and limited attention together, al-
lowing for both reference-dependent preferences and attention. Kovach and Suleymanov
(2023), as discussed before, constructs a model where references affect only the attention.
Bossert and Sprumont (2009) provides another model where reference points don’t affect
preferences. They model a deterministic choice function where the choice is consistent
with not choosing a worse alternative than the reference. They study the existence of a
linear order such that the choice from each menu-reference pair is at least as good as the
reference point, though not necessarily the maximum12. The RAM-UR does have this
non-deteriorating property since references are attention privileged, so in any menu, an
alternative worse than the reference is never chosen.

The idea here is similar to attention privilege as defined by Kovach and Suleymanov
(2023), i.e., if a reference alternative is in the menu, it is always considered. In fact,
that is exactly how I define a reference alternative in this setting. A reference alternative
can have other properties, which maybe correlated with the preferences, dependent upon
some status quo, or some attribute (the color of a car). However, the presented model
is silent on any such dependence. An alternative is a reference if and only if it is atten-
tion privileged, irrespective of how it attained such a privilege. In my model, multiple
reference alternatives or no reference alternatives can be present in any menu, both of
which are not possible in the model presented by Kovach and Suleymanov (2023) since
the primitives there are menu-reference pairs. Note that the default is only chosen in
case none of the alternatives are paid attention to, i.e. if μE(φ, A) > 0. This can only
happen if A ∩E = φ and allows us to interpret the default as a reference.

The fundamental analytical task with respect to the presented model is to identify the
set of reference alternatives and the underlying preferences. In most canonical papers, it
is assumed that the references are observable, which precludes the need to identify the

Kovach and Suleymanov (2023) were able to identify the complete underlying preferences
from the general model with observed references. The RAM-UR works with stochastic
choice functions and the references are unobservable. Given the significant restrictions
to the primitives in this model, it is natural that the preference identification result is
weaker. However, even in the restricted model, quite a significant part of the preferences

respect to the references, unique identification of the preferences among them is achieved.

Soft context compression. Soft context compression offers greater flexibility and expressiveness
than discrete token removal at high compression ratios, and our method belongs to this category.
Wingate et al. presented an early attempt to compress context tokens into a single vector, focusing
on representation learning. AutoCompressor [Chevalier et al., 2023] builds LLMs into compressors
inspired by the Recurrent Memory Transformer [Bulatov et al., 2022], accumulatively compressing
contexts into summary tokens. Mu et al. introduces gist tokens as an information bottleneck by
modifying attention masks, establishing the LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm. ICAE [Ge et al., 2024]
further simplifies this paradigm into an encoder–decoder framework, which has since become a
widely adopted paradigm. Building upon ICAE, 500× [Li et al., 2025c], Activation Beacon [Zhang
et al., 2025], and UniGist [Deng et al., 2025a] pass cached key–value states to the decoder, together
with carefully designed gist-token attention masks, to obtain more informative compressed repre-
sentations. Deng et al. systematically study the effects of different design components within the
encoder–decoder compression framework. EPL [Zhao et al., 2025] further improves compression
performance by adjusting the positional encodings of gist tokens. xRAG [Cheng et al., 2024] explores
converting representations from text embedding models into compression tokens. SAC [Liu et al.,
2026] examines the necessity of the auto-encoding training objective, demonstrating that effective
compression can be achieved using only a text completion objective. Tang et al. [2026] dynamically
assign compression budget through coarse-to-fine compression. Different from the existing methods
that use the internal self-attention mechanisms of LLMs to perform compression, our method adopts
a fundamentally different paradigm by decoupling compression from the LLM architecture and
formulating it as an explicit information transmission problem over frozen hidden states.

Our experiments across 12 datasets show that ComprExIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art CC methods, with an average F1 improvement of 18.5%. It is also lightweight and efficient,
adding only ∼1% parameters while compressing over 2× faster than the fastest baselines. Further
analysis shows that our key design components improve information preservation and thereby boost
compression performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

• We analyze why existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods lose contextual information, and
identify two key bottlenecks: lack of allocation in the width dimension and information
dilution in the depth dimension.
• We propose ComprExIT, a lightweight context compression framework that treats a frozen
LLM as a feature extractor and addresses these bottlenecks with a coordinated widthwise
transmission plan and depthwise layer aggregation.
• We show that ComprExIT consistently outperforms prior context compression methods on
12 datasets, while remaining parameter-efficient and faster at compression.

2
Related Work

Existing context compression methods can be divided into two categories: token pruning and soft
context compression, which operate in discrete and continuous spaces respectively.

Token pruning. Token pruning methods reduce context length by pruning input tokens according
to estimated importance. Representative approaches include SelectiveContext [Li et al., 2023] and
LLMLingua-style methods [Jiang et al., 2023, 2024], which score tokens/spans using a language
model (e.g., via self-information or related salience measures) and retain only the most informative
parts of the context. LLMLingua-2 [Pan et al., 2024] instead distills a lightweight classifier from
a stronger LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to decide which tokens to keep. EFPC [Cao et al., 2025] further
unifies task-aware and task-agnostic compression within a single framework. Despite their efficiency

question: What is the 'layerwise dilution bottleneck' hypothesis discussed around Figure 4?
ground_truth_answer: The layerwise dilution bottleneck hypothesis is that information which is accessible in earlier LLM layers is not fully retained by the time it reaches the final layer's state. This motivates examining how information evolves across both the width and depth dimensions when an LLM is tuned as a compressor, using a probing compressor trained on hidden states from a single chosen layer, evaluated with F1 on SQuAD and HotpotQA.
answer: The “layerwise dilution bottleneck” hypothesis posits that, in a frozen LLM used as a compressor, the usefulness of hidden‑state information does not increase monotonically with depth. Instead, the downstream‑task score ( Sℓ ) often peaks at some intermediate layer and then declines as the model approaches its final layer. This pattern suggests that information that is readily accessible in early or middle layers is **diluted**—i.e., it is not fully retained or propagated to the final hidden state—creating a bottleneck that hampers effective compression [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 4‑5]. The empirical results shown in Figure 4 support this view: many intermediate layers provide strong compression features, while the final layer performs the worst, indicating that useful features formed early are gradually weakened rather than preserved through subsequent transformations [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 4‑5].

5.1
Depthwise Transmission to Token Anchors

5.2
Widthwise Transmission to Compression Slots

Our experiments across 12 datasets show that ComprExIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art CC methods, with an average F1 improvement of 18.5%. It is also lightweight and efficient,
adding only ∼1% parameters while compressing over 2× faster than the fastest baselines. Further
analysis shows that our key design components improve information preservation and thereby boost
compression performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

• We analyze why existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods lose contextual information, and
identify two key bottlenecks: lack of allocation in the width dimension and information
dilution in the depth dimension.
• We propose ComprExIT, a lightweight context compression framework that treats a frozen
LLM as a feature extractor and addresses these bottlenecks with a coordinated widthwise
transmission plan and depthwise layer aggregation.
• We show that ComprExIT consistently outperforms prior context compression methods on
12 datasets, while remaining parameter-efficient and faster at compression.

2
Related Work

Existing context compression methods can be divided into two categories: token pruning and soft
context compression, which operate in discrete and continuous spaces respectively.

Token pruning. Token pruning methods reduce context length by pruning input tokens according
to estimated importance. Representative approaches include SelectiveContext [Li et al., 2023] and
LLMLingua-style methods [Jiang et al., 2023, 2024], which score tokens/spans using a language
model (e.g., via self-information or related salience measures) and retain only the most informative
parts of the context. LLMLingua-2 [Pan et al., 2024] instead distills a lightweight classifier from
a stronger LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to decide which tokens to keep. EFPC [Cao et al., 2025] further
unifies task-aware and task-agnostic compression within a single framework. Despite their efficiency

Abstract

Long-context LLM agents often struggle with growing token, memory, and la-
tency costs, making efficient context compression essential for practical deploy-
ment. Existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods remain noticeably inferior to using
the full context. We find that this gap partly stems from their inability to pre-
serve contextual information effectively. In this work, we revisit context compres-
sion from a structural perspective and identify two key bottlenecks in standard
LLM-based compressors: limited coordination among compression tokens dur-
ing information aggregation, and layerwise dilution that weakens useful signals
from intermediate hidden states. To address these limitations, we propose Com-
prExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a new
context compression framework based on explicit information transmission. Com-
prExIT adaptively aggregates features into anchors across frozen LLM layers,
then allocates information from anchors to compression slots through a globally
coordinated transport plan. Experiments on 12 datasets show that ComprExIT
consistently outperforms strong soft-compression baselines, improving average
F1 by up to 18.5%, while adding only ∼1% trainable parameters and achiev-
ing over 2× faster compression than the fastest baselines. Code is available at
https://github.com/Jiangnan0522/ComprExIT.

question: How is the transmission plan between senders and receiver slots computed in the compression method?
ground_truth_answer: Given a utility matrix and sender/receiver capacities, the transmission plan is obtained by solving an optimization problem that minimizes the total cost, defined as 1 minus the utility, subject to constraints that the assignment mass for each sender sums to its capacity (rho_t) and the mass received by each slot sums to its capacity (rho_k). Unlike self-attention weights, which normalize independently per slot, this formulation couples all sender-slot assignments through shared marginal constraints.
answer:
The method first builds a **utility matrix** \(U_{t,k}\) that measures how beneficial it would be for token‑anchor \(t\) (the sender) to send information to compression slot \(k\) (the receiver).  The utility is computed as the cosine similarity between a projected sender representation and a projected receiver representation (Eq. 7) [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 5‑6, Chunk 5‑6_0011_eedfddd9bf5917da].

Next, each sender is given a **learnable information capacity** \(\rho_t\) by passing its anchor feature through a linear layer and a soft‑max over all anchors (Eq. 8) [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 5‑6, Chunk 5‑6_0011_eedfddd9bf5917da].  All receivers share a uniform capacity \(\rho_k = 1/K\).

With the utility matrix and the sender/receiver capacities, the transmission plan \(\Pi\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K}_{\ge 0}\) is obtained by solving the following **optimal‑transport problem**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\Pi\ge 0}\;&\sum_{t,k}\Pi_{t,k}\,C_{t,k} \\
\text{s.t. }&\sum_{k}\Pi_{t,k}= \rho_t \;\;\forall t,\qquad
\sum_{t}\Pi_{t,k}= \rho_k \;\;\forall k,
\end{aligned}
\]

where the cost is defined as \(C_{t,k}=1-U_{t,k}\) [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 5‑6, Chunk 5‑6_0012_cee88c6df556218b].

Because this objective couples all sender‑slot assignments, its solution is exactly an **entropy‑regularized optimal transport plan** [Villani, 2008].  The authors solve it efficiently with the **Sinkhorn algorithm** (with entropy regularization), running the algorithm on fixed‑size segments (e.g., \(T=128\)) for stability on long sequences [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 5‑6, Chunk 5‑6_0012_cee88c6df556218b].

Thus, the transmission plan is computed by:

1. Computing the utility matrix \(U_{t,k}\).  
2. Determining sender capacities \(\rho_t\) (learned) and uniform receiver capacities \(\rho_k\).  
3. Formulating the marginal‑constrained optimal‑transport problem with cost \(C_{t,k}=1-U_{t,k}\).  
4. Solving it with an entropy‑regularized Sinkhorn iteration to obtain \(\Pi_{t,k}\), which specifies how much information each token anchor sends to each compression slot.

6
Experiments and Analysis

6.1
Experimental Setup

Implementation details. In the experiment, we use Llama-3.2-1B-Base and Llama-3.2-3B-Base
[Grattafiori et al., 2024] as the base model. For the projection to the decoder’s input space, we set
the projection hidden size to 256. The base models are trained using BF16 precision. We employ
the Sinkhorn algorithm with 30 iterations to approximately solve the entropy-regularized optimal
transport problem.

Baselines. We compare with several soft state-of-the-art compression baselines (1) ICAE [Ge et al.,
2024]: a seminal LLM-as-a-compressor method that trains an LLM to encode compressed information
into compression tokens. (2) 500× [Li et al., 2025c]: introduces an extra design that passes the
KV states of the compression tokens to the decoder (3) Activation Beacon [Zhang et al., 2025]:
introduces the interleaving placement of compression tokens. We also include three non-compression
baselines: (4) Zero-shot [w/ context] prompts the LLM with context, serving as an untrained baseline
with zero information loss; (5)Zero-shot [w/o context] prompts the LLM without the context, serving
as an untrained baseline with complete information loss; and (6) Prompt tuning [Lester et al., 2021]
also prepends learnable tokens while retaining full access to the context, and therefore serves as a
strong uncompressed baseline in our experiments.

A.5
Out-of-Domain Results

Table 8 reports the full results on the six out-of-domain MRQA benchmarks. Overall, ComprExIT
remains the strongest compression method across both Llama-3.2-1B-Base and Llama-3.2-3B-Base,
showing that its learned compressed representations transfer well beyond the training domains. We
note that ICAE is competitive on RelationExtraction, whose contexts are very short on average.
Because prior methods use a fixed budget of 128 compression tokens, this dataset effectively gives
them a much smaller compression ratio, which partially explains the smaller gap on that benchmark.

A.6
The Allocation Matrix

Figure 7b visualizes the learned width-wise transmission plan in ComprExIT. Compared with existing
methods (e.g., ICAE in Figure 7a), ComprExIT exhibits a more structured allocation pattern: each
compression slot is softly anchored to a contiguous local region of input tokens, while still retaining
non-negligible connections to distant tokens. This enables ComprExIT to preserve the semantic
order of the context without sacrificing the ability to capture long-range dependencies. In contrast,
although ICAE tries to maintain an order bias (there is a diagonal pattern of high attention values in
Figure Figure 7a), its compression-token attention patterns are weakly localized. Moreover, it can be
observed that some important tokens (e.g. entity “Marcus", number “4.") are ignored collectively by
most of the compression tokens, but some entities (e.g. Broncos) are overly focused. We attribute
these observations to the lack of coordinated allocation.

question: What are the compression and non-compression baselines described on page 6?
ground_truth_answer: The compression baselines include a method that passes KV states of compression tokens to the decoder and Activation Beacon, which introduces interleaved placement of compression tokens. The non-compression baselines are Zero-shot with context (an untrained baseline with zero information loss), Zero-shot without context (an untrained baseline with complete information loss), and Prompt tuning.
answer:
The paper groups the baselines used in the experiments on page 6 as follows:

**Compression baselines**
1. **ICAE** – the “LLM‑as‑a‑compressor” method that trains an LLM to encode information into dedicated compression tokens [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].  
2. **500×** – a method that additionally passes the KV states of the compression tokens to the decoder [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].  
3. **Activation Beacon** – a technique that interleaves compression tokens within the context [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].

**Non‑compression baselines**
1. **Zero‑shot [w/ context]** – prompts the LLM with the full context, acting as an untrained baseline with no information loss [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].  
2. **Zero‑shot [w/o context]** – prompts the LLM without any context, serving as an untrained baseline with complete information loss [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].  
3. **Prompt‑tuning** (Lester et al., 2021) – prepends learnable tokens while still giving the model full access to the context, providing a strong uncompressed baseline [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 6].

transport problem.

Baselines. We compare with several soft state-of-the-art compression baselines (1) ICAE [Ge et al.,
2024]: a seminal LLM-as-a-compressor method that trains an LLM to encode compressed information
into compression tokens. (2) 500× [Li et al., 2025c]: introduces an extra design that passes the
KV states of the compression tokens to the decoder (3) Activation Beacon [Zhang et al., 2025]:
introduces the interleaving placement of compression tokens. We also include three non-compression
baselines: (4) Zero-shot [w/ context] prompts the LLM with context, serving as an untrained baseline
with zero information loss; (5)Zero-shot [w/o context] prompts the LLM without the context, serving
as an untrained baseline with complete information loss; and (6) Prompt tuning [Lester et al., 2021]
also prepends learnable tokens while retaining full access to the context, and therefore serves as a
strong uncompressed baseline in our experiments.

Out-of-domain performance. Using the same training recipe and experimental setup, we further
evaluate on six out-of-domain MRQA datasets in Table 8. ComprExIT again performs best over-
all, improving average F1 over the strongest compression baseline by 30.97% on Llama-3.2-1B
and 14.27% on Llama-3.2-3B, with only a small gap to ICAE on RelationExtraction. Since Rela-
tionExtraction has very short contexts (30 tokens on average) and ICAE and 500x employ a fixed
budget of 128 compression tokens, they are constrained by a much lower compression ratio on this
dataset, thereby yielding better performance. We also evaluate on summarization, fact-checking, and
in-context learning in Appendix A.4. ComprExIT outperforms the uncompressed baseline on XSum
summarization and FEVER fact-checking while remaining competitive on SST-2 in-context learning.
Together, these results suggest that ComprExIT generalizes well to various domains.

6.3
Ablation Studies

We examine our design choices under the same training and evaluation setup as before with Llama-
3.2-1B. To isolate the effect of coordinated allocation, we replace the OT-based allocation module
with a window attention mechanism that preserves locality but removes global coordination. As
shown in Table 2, performance drops consistently across all datasets, indicating that global allocation
is critical for effective compression. Next, we remove layer-wise aggregation and use features from
only a single LLM layer for compression. Performance degrades under all single-layer settings, with
the middle layer (Layer 9) incurring the smallest drop. This result further validates that the design in
ComprExIT that selectively aggregates features from all layers benefit compression.

A.5
Out-of-Domain Results

Our experiments across 12 datasets show that ComprExIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art CC methods, with an average F1 improvement of 18.5%. It is also lightweight and efficient,
adding only ∼1% parameters while compressing over 2× faster than the fastest baselines. Further
analysis shows that our key design components improve information preservation and thereby boost
compression performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

• We analyze why existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods lose contextual information, and
identify two key bottlenecks: lack of allocation in the width dimension and information
dilution in the depth dimension.
• We propose ComprExIT, a lightweight context compression framework that treats a frozen
LLM as a feature extractor and addresses these bottlenecks with a coordinated widthwise
transmission plan and depthwise layer aggregation.
• We show that ComprExIT consistently outperforms prior context compression methods on
12 datasets, while remaining parameter-efficient and faster at compression.

2
Related Work

Existing context compression methods can be divided into two categories: token pruning and soft
context compression, which operate in discrete and continuous spaces respectively.

Token pruning. Token pruning methods reduce context length by pruning input tokens according
to estimated importance. Representative approaches include SelectiveContext [Li et al., 2023] and
LLMLingua-style methods [Jiang et al., 2023, 2024], which score tokens/spans using a language
model (e.g., via self-information or related salience measures) and retain only the most informative
parts of the context. LLMLingua-2 [Pan et al., 2024] instead distills a lightweight classifier from
a stronger LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to decide which tokens to keep. EFPC [Cao et al., 2025] further
unifies task-aware and task-agnostic compression within a single framework. Despite their efficiency

A.5
Out-of-Domain Results

Table 8 reports the full results on the six out-of-domain MRQA benchmarks. Overall, ComprExIT
remains the strongest compression method across both Llama-3.2-1B-Base and Llama-3.2-3B-Base,
showing that its learned compressed representations transfer well beyond the training domains. We
note that ICAE is competitive on RelationExtraction, whose contexts are very short on average.
Because prior methods use a fixed budget of 128 compression tokens, this dataset effectively gives
them a much smaller compression ratio, which partially explains the smaller gap on that benchmark.

A.6
The Allocation Matrix

Figure 7b visualizes the learned width-wise transmission plan in ComprExIT. Compared with existing
methods (e.g., ICAE in Figure 7a), ComprExIT exhibits a more structured allocation pattern: each
compression slot is softly anchored to a contiguous local region of input tokens, while still retaining
non-negligible connections to distant tokens. This enables ComprExIT to preserve the semantic
order of the context without sacrificing the ability to capture long-range dependencies. In contrast,
although ICAE tries to maintain an order bias (there is a diagonal pattern of high attention values in
Figure Figure 7a), its compression-token attention patterns are weakly localized. Moreover, it can be
observed that some important tokens (e.g. entity “Marcus", number “4.") are ignored collectively by
most of the compression tokens, but some entities (e.g. Broncos) are overly focused. We attribute
these observations to the lack of coordinated allocation.

Training

A.8.1
Optimization Behavior

We plot the NTP training curves in Figure 8. ComprExIT starts from the lowest loss and converges
faster to the best plateau, indicating a smaller compressor-decoder mismatch and easier optimization.
This supports our core claim that layer aggregation and coordinated allocation produce compressed
states that preserve useful information while remaining decoder-friendly.

Tables 9 to 11 present the hyperparameters we use when training ComprExIT and the baseline
methods.

A.9
Broader Impact

This work studies learned context compression for long-context language models. Its primary
potential benefit is improved efficiency: effective compression can reduce memory usage, latency,
and computational cost while preserving salient information from the original context. In turn, this
may make document-grounded models more accessible to researchers and practitioners with limited
hardware resources, and may reduce the energy required to deploy such systems at scale. More
efficient long-context modeling may also broaden the practical use of language models in settings
where rapid processing of long documents is important, such as literature review, writing assistance,
and educational tools. Gist tokens can also function as encrypted memory or a communication
medium for LLM agents while remaining unreadable to humans.

question: What does the ablation study in Table 2 show about removing allocation or using only a single layer?
ground_truth_answer: On Llama-3.2-1B, removing allocation ('w/o alloc.') drops average EM by about 4.65 and F1 by about 4.61 relative to full ComprExIT (52.34 EM / 66.55 F1). Using only the embedding layer causes the largest drop (about 23.69 EM / 22.06 F1), while using only layer 9 has the smallest drop among single-layer variants (about 3.00 EM / 2.66 F1), and using only the last layer also causes a large drop (about 16.22 EM / 17.20 F1).
answer:
The ablation study reported in Table 2 demonstrates two key findings:

* **Removing the OT‑based allocation module** (replacing it with a window‑attention mechanism that keeps locality but eliminates global coordination) causes a consistent drop in performance on every dataset. This indicates that the global, coordinated allocation of compression slots is essential for effective compression.  

* **Using features from only a single LLM layer** (instead of aggregating across all layers) also hurts performance across all single‑layer settings. The degradation is smallest when the middle layer (Layer 9) is used, but even then the results are worse than the full multi‑layer design, confirming that selective aggregation of features from all layers benefits compression.  

These observations together validate the importance of both global allocation and layer‑wise aggregation in the ComprExIT design.

question: What does the layer-selection analysis (Figure 6-left) reveal about which LLM layers are most useful for compression?

Method

We present our method in computational order: from depthwise to widthwise computation.

5.1
Depthwise Transmission to Token Anchors

We first address the depthwise limitation discussed above, namely the layerwise dilution bottleneck.
In LLM-as-a-compressor methods, useful information must remain accessible after repeated layer
updates before it reaches the final compression states, even though our preliminary analysis suggests
that the accessible utility can peak at intermediate layers. Therefore, we directly read from hidden
states across depths and construct a token anchor at each token position by adaptively selecting and

which mitigates the layerwise dilution bottleneck. Moreover, because the gating is conditioned on

5.2
Widthwise Transmission to Compression Slots

Since the current LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm is built on the standard LLM architecture, this gap
in information retention calls for a structural re-examination. By tracing how information flows in the
compressor LLM, we identify two limitations. In the width dimension, LLMs rely on self-attention to
condense information from all context tokens into the gist tokens. Yet this process suffers from a
Lack of Allocation: each gist token gathers information independently, without coordinating with
the others about which parts of the context they represent. Consequently, multiple gist tokens may
focus on the same regions while others remain under-covered, leading to information loss. In the
depth dimension, LLMs propagate information in a layer-wise accumulative manner. As forward
propagation proceeds, fine-grained evidence captured in earlier layers can become increasingly
entangled with later, more abstract, generation-oriented representations [Zhang et al., 2024, Skean
et al., 2025]. As a result, early-layer features become harder to recover from the final gist-token states,
leading to Information Dilution [Team et al., 2026b].

The analysis above motivates a different formulation: instead of tuning an LLM into a compressor,
we treat it as a frozen feature extractor and directly use its hidden states for compression. We
propose ComprExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a new context
compression framework that decomposes compression into two stages, each addressing one of the
limitations above. The Widthwise Stage is built around an optimal-transport-based [Villani, 2008]
transmission plan that globally allocates information across tokens and explicitly coordinates how
contextual information is distributed to compression slots. The Depthwise Stage establishes weighted
shortcuts across layers, where fine-grained features extracted at different levels are directly aggregated,
thereby mitigating information dilution across layers.

Conclusion

This work presents ComprExIT, a new paradigm for soft context compression that formulates
compression as explicit information transmission over frozen LLM hidden states, mitigating the

Soft context compression. Soft context compression offers greater flexibility and expressiveness
than discrete token removal at high compression ratios, and our method belongs to this category.
Wingate et al. presented an early attempt to compress context tokens into a single vector, focusing
on representation learning. AutoCompressor [Chevalier et al., 2023] builds LLMs into compressors
inspired by the Recurrent Memory Transformer [Bulatov et al., 2022], accumulatively compressing
contexts into summary tokens. Mu et al. introduces gist tokens as an information bottleneck by
modifying attention masks, establishing the LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm. ICAE [Ge et al., 2024]
further simplifies this paradigm into an encoder–decoder framework, which has since become a
widely adopted paradigm. Building upon ICAE, 500× [Li et al., 2025c], Activation Beacon [Zhang
et al., 2025], and UniGist [Deng et al., 2025a] pass cached key–value states to the decoder, together
with carefully designed gist-token attention masks, to obtain more informative compressed repre-
sentations. Deng et al. systematically study the effects of different design components within the
encoder–decoder compression framework. EPL [Zhao et al., 2025] further improves compression
performance by adjusting the positional encodings of gist tokens. xRAG [Cheng et al., 2024] explores
converting representations from text embedding models into compression tokens. SAC [Liu et al.,
2026] examines the necessity of the auto-encoding training objective, demonstrating that effective
compression can be achieved using only a text completion objective. Tang et al. [2026] dynamically
assign compression budget through coarse-to-fine compression. Different from the existing methods
that use the internal self-attention mechanisms of LLMs to perform compression, our method adopts
a fundamentally different paradigm by decoupling compression from the LLM architecture and
formulating it as an explicit information transmission problem over frozen hidden states.

Soft context compression. Soft context compression offers greater flexibility and expressiveness
than discrete token removal at high compression ratios, and our method belongs to this category.
Wingate et al. presented an early attempt to compress context tokens into a single vector, focusing
on representation learning. AutoCompressor [Chevalier et al., 2023] builds LLMs into compressors
inspired by the Recurrent Memory Transformer [Bulatov et al., 2022], accumulatively compressing
contexts into summary tokens. Mu et al. introduces gist tokens as an information bottleneck by
modifying attention masks, establishing the LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm. ICAE [Ge et al., 2024]
further simplifies this paradigm into an encoder–decoder framework, which has since become a
widely adopted paradigm. Building upon ICAE, 500× [Li et al., 2025c], Activation Beacon [Zhang
et al., 2025], and UniGist [Deng et al., 2025a] pass cached key–value states to the decoder, together
with carefully designed gist-token attention masks, to obtain more informative compressed repre-
sentations. Deng et al. systematically study the effects of different design components within the
encoder–decoder compression framework. EPL [Zhao et al., 2025] further improves compression
performance by adjusting the positional encodings of gist tokens. xRAG [Cheng et al., 2024] explores
converting representations from text embedding models into compression tokens. SAC [Liu et al.,
2026] examines the necessity of the auto-encoding training objective, demonstrating that effective
compression can be achieved using only a text completion objective. Tang et al. [2026] dynamically
assign compression budget through coarse-to-fine compression. Different from the existing methods
that use the internal self-attention mechanisms of LLMs to perform compression, our method adopts
a fundamentally different paradigm by decoupling compression from the LLM architecture and
formulating it as an explicit information transmission problem over frozen hidden states.
3
Preliminary

Since the current LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm is built on the standard LLM architecture, this gap
in information retention calls for a structural re-examination. By tracing how information flows in the
compressor LLM, we identify two limitations. In the width dimension, LLMs rely on self-attention to
condense information from all context tokens into the gist tokens. Yet this process suffers from a
Lack of Allocation: each gist token gathers information independently, without coordinating with
the others about which parts of the context they represent. Consequently, multiple gist tokens may
focus on the same regions while others remain under-covered, leading to information loss. In the
depth dimension, LLMs propagate information in a layer-wise accumulative manner. As forward
propagation proceeds, fine-grained evidence captured in earlier layers can become increasingly
entangled with later, more abstract, generation-oriented representations [Zhang et al., 2024, Skean
et al., 2025]. As a result, early-layer features become harder to recover from the final gist-token states,
leading to Information Dilution [Team et al., 2026b].

The analysis above motivates a different formulation: instead of tuning an LLM into a compressor,
we treat it as a frozen feature extractor and directly use its hidden states for compression. We
propose ComprExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a new context
compression framework that decomposes compression into two stages, each addressing one of the
limitations above. The Widthwise Stage is built around an optimal-transport-based [Villani, 2008]
transmission plan that globally allocates information across tokens and explicitly coordinates how
contextual information is distributed to compression slots. The Depthwise Stage establishes weighted
shortcuts across layers, where fine-grained features extracted at different levels are directly aggregated,
thereby mitigating information dilution across layers.

question: How does ComprExIT perform on the out-of-domain MRQA benchmarks compared to ICAE?
ground_truth_answer: ComprExIT remains the strongest compression method across both Llama-3.2-1B-Base and Llama-3.2-3B-Base on the six out-of-domain MRQA benchmarks, showing its learned compressed representations transfer well beyond the training domains. ICAE is noted as competitive specifically on the RelationExtraction dataset, whose contexts are very short on average, which effectively gives it a larger compression-token budget relative to context length since prior methods use a fixed budget of 128 compression tokens.
answer:
ComprExIT is the top‑performing compression method on all six out‑of‑domain MRQA benchmarks.  
* Across both Llama‑3.2‑1B‑Base and Llama‑3.2‑3B‑Base models it “remains the strongest compression method…showing that its learned compressed representations transfer well beyond the training domains” [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 16].  
* Using the same training recipe, it “improves average F1 over the strongest compression baseline by 30.97 % on Llama‑3.2‑1B and 14.27 % on Llama‑3.2‑3B” [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 7‑8].  
* The detailed results in Table 8 confirm that ComprExIT attains higher EM and F1 scores than ICAE on virtually every dataset (e.g., on BioASQ F1 74.96 vs 75.97 for ICAE on Llama‑3.2‑1B, on DROP F1 50.73 vs 34.60, etc.) [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 16‑17].  

The only case where ICAE is close to or slightly ahead of ComprExIT is the **RelationExtraction** benchmark, where contexts are very short (≈30 tokens). Because ICAE (and the 500× baseline) use a fixed budget of 128 compression tokens, they enjoy a higher effective compression ratio on this dataset, narrowing the gap [Context_Compression.pdf, Page 16].  

In summary, ComprExIT consistently outperforms ICAE on the out‑of‑domain MRQA benchmarks, delivering substantially higher F1 scores overall, with the exception of a modestly smaller advantage on the short‑context RelationExtraction task.

question: What broader efficiency benefits does the paper claim for effective context compression?
ground_truth_answer: The paper states that effective compression can reduce memory usage, latency, and computational cost while preserving salient information from the original context, which may make document-grounded models more accessible to researchers and practitioners with limited hardware resources and could broaden the practical use of language models in resource-constrained settings.
answer:
The paper states that effective context compression can bring several efficiency‑related advantages:

* **Reduced memory usage** – compressing the context means fewer tokens need to be stored in GPU memory.  
* **Lower latency** – shorter compressed representations can be processed more quickly, cutting inference time.  
* **Lower computational cost** – fewer tokens and lighter processing reduce the amount of compute required per request.  
* **Energy savings** – because less compute is needed, the overall energy consumption for deploying long‑context models is decreased.  
* **Greater accessibility** – the reduced resource demands make document‑grounded models usable on more modest hardware, expanding who can run them.  

These benefits are described in the “Broader Impact” section of the paper [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 18‑19].

Broader Impact

This work studies learned context compression for long-context language models. Its primary
potential benefit is improved efficiency: effective compression can reduce memory usage, latency,
and computational cost while preserving salient information from the original context. In turn, this
may make document-grounded models more accessible to researchers and practitioners with limited
hardware resources, and may reduce the energy required to deploy such systems at scale. More
efficient long-context modeling may also broaden the practical use of language models in settings
where rapid processing of long documents is important, such as literature review, writing assistance,
and educational tools. Gist tokens can also function as encrypted memory or a communication
medium for LLM agents while remaining unreadable to humans.

Our experiments across 12 datasets show that ComprExIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art CC methods, with an average F1 improvement of 18.5%. It is also lightweight and efficient,
adding only ∼1% parameters while compressing over 2× faster than the fastest baselines. Further
analysis shows that our key design components improve information preservation and thereby boost
compression performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

• We analyze why existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods lose contextual information, and
identify two key bottlenecks: lack of allocation in the width dimension and information
dilution in the depth dimension.
• We propose ComprExIT, a lightweight context compression framework that treats a frozen
LLM as a feature extractor and addresses these bottlenecks with a coordinated widthwise
transmission plan and depthwise layer aggregation.
• We show that ComprExIT consistently outperforms prior context compression methods on
12 datasets, while remaining parameter-efficient and faster at compression.

2
Related Work

Existing context compression methods can be divided into two categories: token pruning and soft
context compression, which operate in discrete and continuous spaces respectively.

Token pruning. Token pruning methods reduce context length by pruning input tokens according
to estimated importance. Representative approaches include SelectiveContext [Li et al., 2023] and
LLMLingua-style methods [Jiang et al., 2023, 2024], which score tokens/spans using a language
model (e.g., via self-information or related salience measures) and retain only the most informative
parts of the context. LLMLingua-2 [Pan et al., 2024] instead distills a lightweight classifier from
a stronger LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to decide which tokens to keep. EFPC [Cao et al., 2025] further
unifies task-aware and task-agnostic compression within a single framework. Despite their efficiency

At the same time, context compression introduces important risks. Any compression method may
discard rare but critical details, qualifiers, or provenance signals, which can lead to overconfident
but incomplete answers. Such failures may be especially concerning in high-stakes applications
such as medicine, law, science, or public policy, where omitted evidence can materially affect the
correct conclusion. In addition, compressed-context models can still inherit social biases, factual
errors, and privacy risks from their pretrained backbone and training data, and efficient processing of
long documents could be misused for large-scale analysis of sensitive text. We therefore recommend
task-specific evaluation, preserving access to the original context whenever possible, and avoiding
deployment as a substitute for expert judgment in safety-critical settings.

Soft context compression. Soft context compression offers greater flexibility and expressiveness
than discrete token removal at high compression ratios, and our method belongs to this category.
Wingate et al. presented an early attempt to compress context tokens into a single vector, focusing
on representation learning. AutoCompressor [Chevalier et al., 2023] builds LLMs into compressors
inspired by the Recurrent Memory Transformer [Bulatov et al., 2022], accumulatively compressing
contexts into summary tokens. Mu et al. introduces gist tokens as an information bottleneck by
modifying attention masks, establishing the LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm. ICAE [Ge et al., 2024]
further simplifies this paradigm into an encoder–decoder framework, which has since become a
widely adopted paradigm. Building upon ICAE, 500× [Li et al., 2025c], Activation Beacon [Zhang
et al., 2025], and UniGist [Deng et al., 2025a] pass cached key–value states to the decoder, together
with carefully designed gist-token attention masks, to obtain more informative compressed repre-
sentations. Deng et al. systematically study the effects of different design components within the
encoder–decoder compression framework. EPL [Zhao et al., 2025] further improves compression
performance by adjusting the positional encodings of gist tokens. xRAG [Cheng et al., 2024] explores
converting representations from text embedding models into compression tokens. SAC [Liu et al.,
2026] examines the necessity of the auto-encoding training objective, demonstrating that effective
compression can be achieved using only a text completion objective. Tang et al. [2026] dynamically
assign compression budget through coarse-to-fine compression. Different from the existing methods
that use the internal self-attention mechanisms of LLMs to perform compression, our method adopts
a fundamentally different paradigm by decoupling compression from the LLM architecture and
formulating it as an explicit information transmission problem over frozen hidden states.

Abstract

Long-context LLM agents often struggle with growing token, memory, and la-
tency costs, making efficient context compression essential for practical deploy-
ment. Existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods remain noticeably inferior to using
the full context. We find that this gap partly stems from their inability to pre-
serve contextual information effectively. In this work, we revisit context compres-
sion from a structural perspective and identify two key bottlenecks in standard
LLM-based compressors: limited coordination among compression tokens dur-
ing information aggregation, and layerwise dilution that weakens useful signals
from intermediate hidden states. To address these limitations, we propose Com-
prExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a new
context compression framework based on explicit information transmission. Com-
prExIT adaptively aggregates features into anchors across frozen LLM layers,
then allocates information from anchors to compression slots through a globally
coordinated transport plan. Experiments on 12 datasets show that ComprExIT
consistently outperforms strong soft-compression baselines, improving average
F1 by up to 18.5%, while adding only ∼1% trainable parameters and achiev-
ing over 2× faster compression than the fastest baselines. Code is available at
https://github.com/Jiangnan0522/ComprExIT.

question: What theoretical support does the paper provide for the idea of information dilution across layers?
ground_truth_answer: The paper argues that even if each layer introduces only a modest shift, the total drift can still grow with network depth and effectively increase M, making the compression objective harder to optimize; this claim is backed both by a theoretical result in Appendix A.7/A.8 and by the extensive experiments in Section 3 and the appendix.
answer:
The paper backs the “information‑dilution” intuition with a formal bound on how representation drift accumulates as a signal passes through successive transformer layers.  

In Appendix A the authors model the encoder as a sequence of stochastic compressors \(p(Z(0)),\dots ,p(Z(L))\) and define the final compressor–decoder mismatch \(M\) as a Wasserstein distance between the distribution at the last layer and the decoder’s expected distribution \(p_{\text{dec}}\) [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 17‑18].  

Proposition A.1 (Accumulation of layerwise drift) shows that, under mild moment assumptions, the total mismatch is bounded by the sum of the initial mismatch at the encoder input and the cumulative drift incurred at each layer:

\[
M \;\le\; W\bigl(p(Z(0)),p_{\text{dec}}\bigr) \;+\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1} W\bigl(p(Z(\ell+1)),p(Z(\ell))\bigr).
\]

The proof repeatedly applies the triangle inequality for the Wasserstein distance, yielding the bound above [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 17‑18].  

Because each layer can introduce even a modest shift, the cumulative term can grow with depth, increasing the overall mismatch \(M\). This formal result demonstrates that “layerwise drift” – i.e., the gradual loss or transformation of information as it propagates through layers – can become significant in deep models, providing theoretical support for the observed information‑dilution phenomenon. [Context_Compression.pdf, Pages 17‑18]

The proposition shows that the final mismatch is upper-bounded by two terms: the initial mismatch
at the compressor input, and the cumulative layerwise drift accrued across the encoder. Therefore,
even if each layer introduces only a modest shift, the total drift can still grow with depth, increase M,
and make the compression objective harder to optimize. Together with the extensive experiments
in Sections 3 and Appendix A, this provides both theoretical and empirical support for the role of
information dilution.

A.8
Training

A.8.1
Optimization Behavior

Since the current LLM-as-a-compressor paradigm is built on the standard LLM architecture, this gap
in information retention calls for a structural re-examination. By tracing how information flows in the
compressor LLM, we identify two limitations. In the width dimension, LLMs rely on self-attention to
condense information from all context tokens into the gist tokens. Yet this process suffers from a
Lack of Allocation: each gist token gathers information independently, without coordinating with
the others about which parts of the context they represent. Consequently, multiple gist tokens may
focus on the same regions while others remain under-covered, leading to information loss. In the
depth dimension, LLMs propagate information in a layer-wise accumulative manner. As forward
propagation proceeds, fine-grained evidence captured in earlier layers can become increasingly
entangled with later, more abstract, generation-oriented representations [Zhang et al., 2024, Skean
et al., 2025]. As a result, early-layer features become harder to recover from the final gist-token states,
leading to Information Dilution [Team et al., 2026b].

The analysis above motivates a different formulation: instead of tuning an LLM into a compressor,
we treat it as a frozen feature extractor and directly use its hidden states for compression. We
propose ComprExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a new context
compression framework that decomposes compression into two stages, each addressing one of the
limitations above. The Widthwise Stage is built around an optimal-transport-based [Villani, 2008]
transmission plan that globally allocates information across tokens and explicitly coordinates how
contextual information is distributed to compression slots. The Depthwise Stage establishes weighted
shortcuts across layers, where fine-grained features extracted at different levels are directly aggregated,
thereby mitigating information dilution across layers.

7
Conclusion

This work presents ComprExIT, a new paradigm for soft context compression that formulates
compression as explicit information transmission over frozen LLM hidden states, mitigating the
limitations of layerwise dilution and lack of allocation. Experiments show that it consistently
outperforms prior compression methods. More broadly, the proposed paradigm provides a more
flexible design space beyond standard attention-based formulations. Therefore, we hope that this
work can inspire future research to explore more design choices in this new paradigm and further
advance context compression research.

Limitations. First, due to limited computational resources, we do not test ComprExIT on larger
backbones (e.g., 32B or 70B models) or substantially longer contexts (e.g., 32k or 128k tokens).
Second, our experiments focus on text-only language models. Extending the framework to vision-
language models, which also accepts tokenized inputs, is left to future work.

A.8
Training

A.8.1
Optimization Behavior

We plot the NTP training curves in Figure 8. ComprExIT starts from the lowest loss and converges
faster to the best plateau, indicating a smaller compressor-decoder mismatch and easier optimization.
This supports our core claim that layer aggregation and coordinated allocation produce compressed
states that preserve useful information while remaining decoder-friendly.

A.8.2
Training Details

Tables 9 to 11 present the hyperparameters we use when training ComprExIT and the baseline
methods.

A.9
Broader Impact

This work studies learned context compression for long-context language models. Its primary
potential benefit is improved efficiency: effective compression can reduce memory usage, latency,
and computational cost while preserving salient information from the original context. In turn, this
may make document-grounded models more accessible to researchers and practitioners with limited
hardware resources, and may reduce the energy required to deploy such systems at scale. More
efficient long-context modeling may also broaden the practical use of language models in settings
where rapid processing of long documents is important, such as literature review, writing assistance,
and educational tools. Gist tokens can also function as encrypted memory or a communication
medium for LLM agents while remaining unreadable to humans.

Out-of-domain performance. Using the same training recipe and experimental setup, we further
evaluate on six out-of-domain MRQA datasets in Table 8. ComprExIT again performs best over-
all, improving average F1 over the strongest compression baseline by 30.97% on Llama-3.2-1B
and 14.27% on Llama-3.2-3B, with only a small gap to ICAE on RelationExtraction. Since Rela-
tionExtraction has very short contexts (30 tokens on average) and ICAE and 500x employ a fixed
budget of 128 compression tokens, they are constrained by a much lower compression ratio on this
dataset, thereby yielding better performance. We also evaluate on summarization, fact-checking, and
in-context learning in Appendix A.4. ComprExIT outperforms the uncompressed baseline on XSum
summarization and FEVER fact-checking while remaining competitive on SST-2 in-context learning.
Together, these results suggest that ComprExIT generalizes well to various domains.

6.3
Ablation Studies

We examine our design choices under the same training and evaluation setup as before with Llama-
3.2-1B. To isolate the effect of coordinated allocation, we replace the OT-based allocation module
with a window attention mechanism that preserves locality but removes global coordination. As
shown in Table 2, performance drops consistently across all datasets, indicating that global allocation
is critical for effective compression. Next, we remove layer-wise aggregation and use features from
only a single LLM layer for compression. Performance degrades under all single-layer settings, with
the middle layer (Layer 9) incurring the smallest drop. This result further validates that the design in
ComprExIT that selectively aggregates features from all layers benefit compression.

At the same time, context compression introduces important risks. Any compression method may
discard rare but critical details, qualifiers, or provenance signals, which can lead to overconfident
but incomplete answers. Such failures may be especially concerning in high-stakes applications
such as medicine, law, science, or public policy, where omitted evidence can materially affect the
correct conclusion. In addition, compressed-context models can still inherit social biases, factual
errors, and privacy risks from their pretrained backbone and training data, and efficient processing of
long documents could be misused for large-scale analysis of sensitive text. We therefore recommend
task-specific evaluation, preserving access to the original context whenever possible, and avoiding
deployment as a substitute for expert judgment in safety-critical settings.
